Jay Leno Drives Jerry O'Connell's 1979 Cadillac Seville, Stolen From His Driveway and Recovered
13 photos
Photo: Jay Leno's Garage | YouTube
Actor Jerry O’Connell took his 1979 Cadillac Seville to Jay Leno’s Garage to brag about it and to tell the story of how it was stolen from his driveway in California, pulled over for speeding, and recovered a few hours later, even before the actor realized it was missing.
The 1979 Cadillac Seville was stolen from Jerry O'Connell's driveway in Calabasas, California, on January 13 or 14, 2026, and recovered by law enforcement soon after the theft. The perpetrator got their hands on it while Jerry O’Connell and his wife, Rebecca Romijn, were out of town.
He had to pay for three days of impound, until authorities completed the investigation. The impound lot's chalk marks are still on the rear window. He later admitted he had left the keys inside the center console, so it was easy for the thief to drive off in it.
Deputies from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department in Malibu pulled the car over for speeding at around 90 mph (145 kph). They found it hard to believe that a man like that would drive such a car. The thief was on a joyride on the Pacific Coast Highway.
When questioned, the driver claimed the vintage car belonged to him and grabbed whatever was in the glove box and handed it over as a bluff. Deputies ran the vehicle's registration, called the owner, and told him it had been stolen. The man was arrested, booked at the Malibu/Lost Hills Station, and later released on a promise to appear in court.
Days after the incident, O'Connell hilariously cleared up any confusion on social media, repeatedly posting headlines of the incident and telling his followers: " Just to be clear, I am not the homeless man in this story ."
Officers safely returned the car to its rightful owner, who publicly thanked the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department on social media, taking full responsibility for leaving the keys inside. That’s something he no longer does. He had never driven as fast as the thief before, but he is doing it now.
His Cadillac luxury sedan , finished in light blue, is his daily commuter car. He found it on Craigslist, where an older gentleman had it listed for sale for $16,000. He negotiated with the seller and eventually took it home for $12,000.
His wife, Rebecca, always acts as the witness during his strict classic-car buying process, which mandates only cars sold on Craigslist, located within 50 miles (80 kilometers) of home, and only models between 1960 and 1991.
He is 52 now, and Rebecca says he is only looking for cars rich people had when he was a child. He never buys a car she doesn’t approve of. His kids don’t get sick when they ride in the back, so that, along with the comfort and luxury it provides, convinced him to use it as a daily driver.
And speaking of comfort, Jerry sits on a wooden bead seat cushion. " There is nobody under the age of 70 sitting on one of these, " says 76-year-old Jay Leno . Jerry says he no longer drives without it. It's not just about comfort. The truth is that the driver's seat has started to show its age and he is masking it with the wooden bead seat cushion.
Jerry admits he washed the car for the show, but failed to clean the engine bay. “It’s the dustiest engine compartment I’ve ever seen,” Leno scolds him. “Are you driving in the desert or somewhere?” It actually looks like the engine compartment of a daily driver. Garaged collector cars that are only driven every once in a while are obviously far cleaner.
No wonder the Cadillac Seville got the homeless man's attention. The 1979 model year marked the grand finale for the first generation. When it debuted, the Cadillac-badged luxo-barge basically flipped American luxury car design on its head.
In the mid-1970s, American luxury meant massive land yachts. Cadillac introduced the Seville to fight back against rising European imports from luxury carmakers such as Mercedes-Benz and BMW. The Seville was 27 inches shorter and 1,000 pounds lighter than the standard DeVille.
Despite being far smaller, it was actually the automaker’s most expensive production car at the time, carrying a base price of roughly $15,600. Adjusted for inflation, that would be approximately $70,000 in today’s money.
The Seville was way ahead of its time. It pioneered GM’s early electronic fuel injection system and was available with the then-new digital Trip Computer dashboard, offered for extra money. A rear defogger and cruise control were also on the menu.
Powering the Seville is a 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) Oldsmobile Rocket V8 engine , which pushes out 170 horsepower (172 metric horsepower) and 270 pound-feet (366 Newton meters) of torque. A three-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic automatic transmission puts the power down through the rear wheels.
The Seville took forever to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill: it needed 13 seconds for the run on its way to a top speed of 115 mph (185 kph). But the Seville was more about luxury than about performance.
The car measures 204.0 inches (5,182 millimeters) in length, 71.8 inches (1,824 millimeters) in width, 54.7 inches (1,389 millimeters) in height, sitting on a wheelbase of 114.3 inches (2,903 millimeters). The Seville tips the scales at 4,180 pounds (1,896 kilograms).
That is what Jay Leno takes to the streets of Los Angeles. The suspension of the 47-year-old luxury sedan absorbs all the road imperfections for a plush-like ride, providing what Leno calls " a boulevard ride ."
" It's got some power, it’s kind of fun ," he says about the V8-powered luxo-barge from the 1970s. However, he doesn't go over 60 mph (97 kph). He won't drive it like he stole it.
